claim: Regional stability across distant local communities was related to stability and asynchrony of local communities in Inner Mongolian grassland.
source: We found that regional stability across distant local communities was related to stability and asynchrony of local communities.
evidence: Supported by path analysis models showing positive relationships between regional community CV and local community CV and regional community synchrony (Figure 2a and b, Figure 3a).

claim: Using only dominant instead of all-species dynamics explained regional stability almost equally well.
source: Using only dominant instead of all-species dynamics explained regional stability almost equally well.
evidence: Supported by comparison of explanatory power between all-species (R²=0.98) and dominant-species (R²=0.71 and 0.69) measures in Figure 3.

claim: The diversity of all or only dominant species had comparatively weak effects on stability and synchrony.
source: The diversity of all or only dominant species had comparatively weak effects on stability and synchrony
evidence: Supported by weak or non-significant relationships shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A lower mean precipitation destabilized regional and local communities by reducing population stability.
source: whereas a lower mean and higher variation of precipitation destabilized regional and local communities by reducing population stability and synchronizing species dynamics.
evidence: Supported by path analysis showing negative effect of precipitation on local population CV in Figure 3b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Higher variation of precipitation destabilized regional and local communities by synchronizing species dynamics.
source: whereas a lower mean and higher variation of precipitation destabilized regional and local communities by reducing population stability and synchronizing species dynamics.
evidence: Supported by path analysis showing positive effect of precipitation CV on local species synchrony in Figure 3a and Figure 4h.

claim: For semi-arid temperate grassland with highly uneven species abundances, the stability of regional communities is increased by stability and asynchrony of local communities.
source: We demonstrate that, for semi-arid temperate grassland with highly uneven species abundances, the stability of regional communities is increased by stability and asynchrony of local communities and these are more affected by climate rather than species diversity.
evidence: Supported by path analysis results in Figure 3 showing relationships between regional and local community stability and asynchrony.

claim: Regional community stability is more affected by climate rather than species diversity in semi-arid temperate grassland with highly uneven species abundances.
source: We demonstrate that, for semi-arid temperate grassland with highly uneven species abundances, the stability of regional communities is increased by stability and asynchrony of local communities and these are more affected by climate rather than species diversity.
evidence: Supported by stronger effects of precipitation variables compared to diversity indices in path analysis models (Figure 3).

claim: Reduced amounts and increased variation of precipitation in the future may compromise the sustainable provision of ecosystem services to human well-being in Inner Mongolian grassland.
source: Reduced amounts and increased variation of precipitation in the future may compromise the sustainable provision of ecosystem services to human well-being in this region.
evidence: Based on observed negative effects of precipitation changes on stability and known precipitation trends in the region.

claim: The ability of ecosystems to stably provide biological products and services is being threatened by species loss.
source: The ability of ecosystems to stably provide biological products and services such as biomass production for human well-being (Isbell et al., 2015; Tilman et al., 2014, Tilman et al., 2006) is being threatened by species loss (Cardinale et al., 2012; Harrison et al., 2015; Isbell et al., 2017; Isbell et al., 2015; Newbold et al., 2015; Tilman et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The ability of ecosystems to stably provide biological products and services is being threatened by climate change.
source: The ability of ecosystems to stably provide biological products and services such as biomass production for human well-being (Isbell et al., 2015; Tilman et al., 2014, Tilman et al., 2006) is being threatened by species loss (Cardinale et al., 2012; Harrison et al., 2015; Isbell et al., 2017; Isbell et al., 2015; Newbold et al., 2015; Tilman et al., 2014) and climate change (Hautier et al., 2015; Hautier et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Previous theoretical, experimental, and observational studies on ecosystem stability have mostly been conducted at local scales with homogenous environmental conditions.
source: However, previous theoretical, experimental, and observational studies on ecosystem stability have mostly been conducted at local scales with homogenous environmental conditions (Hautier et al., 2015; Hautier et al., 2014; Hector et al., 2010; Isbell et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2017; Tilman et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Patterns of ecosystem stability discovered in local communities may not directly scale up to a system of spatially separate communities.
source: Patterns of ecosystem stability discovered in local communities may not directly scale up to a system of spatially separate communities (Lamy et al., 2019; McGranahan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Wang and Loreau, 2016; Wang and Loreau, 2014; Wilcox et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There is an urgent need to understand stability and the factors maintaining it at spatial scales covering larger areas.
source: Thus, there is an urgent need to understand stability and the factors maintaining it at spatial scales covering larger areas (Gonzalez et al., 2020; Isbell et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical inference from previous statements about limitations of local-scale studies.

claim: Local asynchronous species dynamics stabilize local communities through species insurance effect.
source: Along pathway I, local asynchronous species dynamics stabilize local communities (step A, species insurance effect of local species asynchrony; Yachi and Loreau, 1999)
evidence: Theoretical framework cited from published literature.

claim: Asynchronous community dynamics among distant localities stabilize regional communities through spatial insurance effect.
source: and asynchronous community dynamics among distant localities stabilize regional communities (step B, spatial insurance effect of regional community asynchrony; Wang and Loreau, 2016; Wang and Loreau, 2014).
evidence: Theoretical framework cited from published literature.

claim: Asynchronous population dynamics within species among distant localities stabilize regional populations through spatial insurance effect.
source: Along pathway II, asynchronous population dynamics within species among distant localities stabilize regional populations (step A, spatial insurance effect of regional population asynchrony; Wang and Loreau, 2016; Wang and Loreau, 2014)
evidence: Theoretical framework cited from published literature.

claim: Regional asynchronous species dynamics stabilize regional communities through species insurance effect.
source: and regional asynchronous species dynamics stabilize regional communities (step B, species insurance effect of regional species asynchrony; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Theoretical framework cited from published literature.

claim: Species diversity has been hypothesized to stabilize ecosystems at different ecological hierarchies because species-rich communities are more likely to include species that have different responses to environmental variation across time and space.
source: Species diversity has been hypothesized to stabilize ecosystems at different ecological hierarchies because species-rich communities are more likely to include species that have different responses to environmental variation across time and space, producing stable communities via species asynchrony (Thibaut and Connolly, 2013; Tilman et al., 2014; Wang and Loreau, 2016; Wang and Loreau, 2014; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The role of species diversity in affecting stability across different ecological hierarchies is still unclear in natural ecosystems.
source: In natural ecosystems, the role of species diversity in affecting stability across different ecological hierarchies is still unclear.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Theoretical and experimental studies propose stabilizing effects of alpha diversity within local communities.
source: Theoretical and experimental studies propose stabilizing effects of (alpha) diversity within local communities (Hautier et al., 2015; Hautier et al., 2014; Hector et al., 2010; Tilman et al., 2014; Tilman et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Biodiversity experiments usually consider systems in which species abundance distributions are relatively even, at least at the beginning of newly assembled communities.
source: However, these studies usually consider systems in which species abundance distributions are relatively even, at least at the beginning of newly assembled communities in biodiversity experiments (Hector et al., 2010; Tilman et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Natural communities are often characterized by highly uneven abundance distributions and dominated by the dynamics of a few abundant species.
source: Natural communities are often characterized by highly uneven abundance distributions and dominated by the dynamics of a few abundant species (Thibaut and Connolly, 2013; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Sometimes low-abundance species can disproportionately contribute to certain ecosystem functions.
source: even with exceptions that sometimes low-abundance species can disproportionately contribute to certain ecosystem functions (Dee et al., 2019; Leitão et al., 2016; Schmid et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: With highly uneven abundance distributions, the predicted local-scale diversity–stability relationship may be weak.
source: With highly uneven abundance distributions, the predicted local-scale diversity–stability relationship may be weak and it may be sufficient to focus on the population dynamics of dominant species (see Appendix 1 for dominant-species measure) instead of all species (Wang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It may be sufficient to focus on the population dynamics of dominant species instead of all species in communities with highly uneven abundance distributions.
source: With highly uneven abundance distributions, the predicted local-scale diversity–stability relationship may be weak and it may be sufficient to focus on the population dynamics of dominant species (see Appendix 1 for dominant-species measure) instead of all species (Wang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Theoretical studies propose that the heterogeneity in species compositions between distant local communities (beta diversity) can increase asynchronous dynamics among them, resulting in stabilized regional communities.
source: Furthermore, theoretical studies also propose that the heterogeneity in species compositions between distant local communities (beta diversity) can increase asynchronous dynamics among them, resulting in stabilized regional communities (Wang et al., 2019; Wang and Loreau, 2016).
evidence: Theoretical prediction supported by citations.

claim: Empirical evidence for the stabilizing effect of beta diversity is mixed, detected in some but not in other studies.
source: Currently, empirical evidence for such an effect is mixed as it was detected in some (e.g., Hautier et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2021; Qiao et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019) but not in other studies (e.g., Wilcox et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies with contrasting results.

claim: Studies that did not detect beta diversity effects looked at rather small spatial scales with potentially low beta diversity or even the same dominant species occurring among local communities.
source: These studies looked at rather small spatial scales with potentially low beta diversity or even the same dominant species occurring among local communities, making it difficult to detect a stabilizing effect at the regional scale where management decisions are taken.
evidence: Inference about limitations of previous studies.

claim: Asynchrony among local communities with different dominant species may contribute to regional community stability.
source: Because different species may be dominant in distant local communities, asynchrony among these local communities may contribute to regional community stability (Wang et al., 2019; Wang and Loreau, 2016; Wang and Loreau, 2014; Isbell et al., 2018).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The study established a region-scale observation network in Inner Mongolian grassland across an area of >166,894 km².
source: To investigate the temporal stability of aboveground biomass production ('productivity' for short) at larger spatial scales, we established a region-scale observation network in Inner Mongolian grassland in China across an area of >166,894 km2
evidence: Description of study design and methods.

claim: The study monitored yearly dynamics of productivity over five consecutive years.
source: and monitored the yearly dynamics of productivity over five consecutive years (Figure 1a).
evidence: Description of study design with reference to figure.

claim: The Inner Mongolian grassland represents a typical part of the Eurasian grassland biome.
source: The Inner Mongolian grassland represents a typical part of the Eurasian grassland biome and is crucial in providing biological products and services to human societies living there (Fang et al., 2015; Kang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Inner Mongolian grassland is crucial in providing biological products and services to human societies living there.
source: The Inner Mongolian grassland represents a typical part of the Eurasian grassland biome and is crucial in providing biological products and services to human societies living there (Fang et al., 2015; Kang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In Inner Mongolian grassland, plant community productivity and species richness and composition are driven by climatic factors, that is, temperature and precipitation.
source: In this region, plant community productivity and species richness and composition are driven by climatic factors, that is, temperature and precipitation (Bai et al., 2004; Hu et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Temperature and precipitation have changed considerably in Inner Mongolian grassland during the past decades.
source: These have changed considerably during the past decades (Huang et al., 2015; Piao et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ecological consequences of climate change in Inner Mongolian grassland are largely unknown, especially at large spatial scales.
source: with largely unknown ecological consequences, especially at large spatial scales.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge.

claim: The study employed a simulated landscape method to construct large-scale regional communities consisting of two local communities separated by 17–987 km.
source: To facilitate the large-scale stability investigation, we employed a simulated landscape method (Hautier et al., 2018; van der Plas et al., 2016) to construct large-scale, that is, regional communities consisting of two local communities (two observed sites) separated by 17–987 km (Figure 1a).
evidence: Description of study methods with citations and figure reference.

claim: Each regional community was constructed by randomly choosing two distant local communities without replacement.
source: Briefly, each regional community was constructed by randomly choosing two distant local communities without replacement (to ensure replicate regional communities were not sharing local communities; Figure 1b).
evidence: Description of study methods with figure reference.

claim: The study did not consider scenarios including more than two local communities in each regional community because the resulting small number of replicate regional communities would have prevented a statistical analysis.
source: We did not consider scenarios including more than two local communities in each regional community because the resulting small number of replicate regional communities would have prevented a statistical analysis (but see Appendix 1—figure 3 for a three-local-community scenario).
evidence: Explanation of methodological choice.

claim: The regional community CV was positively associated with the local community CV.
source: We found that the regional community CV was positively associated with the local community CV and regional community synchrony (step B of upscaling pathway I; Figure 2a and b, Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The regional community CV was positively associated with regional community synchrony.
source: We found that the regional community CV was positively associated with the local community CV and regional community synchrony (step B of upscaling pathway I; Figure 2a and b, Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The local community CV was positively related to the local population CV.
source: The local community CV in turn was positively related to the local population CV and local species synchrony (step A in upscaling pathways I; Figure 2e and f, Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The local community CV was positively related to local species synchrony.
source: The local community CV in turn was positively related to the local population CV and local species synchrony (step A in upscaling pathways I; Figure 2e and f, Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Along upscaling pathway I, the CVs decreased from 0.76 for the local population CV to 0.38 for the local community CV and further to 0.29 for the regional community CV.
source: Along the upscaling pathway I, the CVs decreased from 0.76 for the local population CV to 0.38 for the local community CV and further to 0.29 for the regional community CV (Figure 3a)
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure.

claim: Local species synchrony (mean = 0.49) was lower compared with regional community synchrony (mean = 0.78).
source: as a result of a lower local species synchrony (mean = 0.49) compared with regional community synchrony (mean = 0.78; Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure.

claim: The regional community CV was positively related to the regional population CV.
source: Alternatively, the regional community CV was positively related to the regional population CV and regional species synchrony (step B of upscaling pathway II; Figure 2c and d, Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The regional community CV was positively related to regional species synchrony.
source: Alternatively, the regional community CV was positively related to the regional population CV and regional species synchrony (step B of upscaling pathway II; Figure 2c and d, Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The regional population CV was positively related to the local population CV.
source: The regional population CV was in turn positively related to the local population CV but not to regional population synchrony (step B of upscaling pathway II; Figure 2g and h).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The regional population CV was not related to regional population synchrony in simple regression analysis.
source: The regional population CV was in turn positively related to the local population CV but not to regional population synchrony (step B of upscaling pathway II; Figure 2g and h).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The path from regional population synchrony to regional population CV became significant in the SEM despite being non-significant in simple regression.
source: However, the path from regional population synchrony to regional population CV was suggested by theory and therefore included in the SEM, where it became significant (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by path analysis results shown in figure.

claim: Along upscaling pathway II, the CVs declined from 0.76 for the local population CV to 0.71 for the regional population CV and further to 0.29 for the regional community CV.
source: Along the upscaling pathway II, the CVs declined from 0.76 for the local population CV to 0.71 for the regional population CV and further to 0.29 for the regional community CV (Figure 3a)
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure.

claim: Regional population synchrony (mean = 0.94) was higher compared with regional species synchrony (mean = 0.41).
source: as a result of a higher regional population synchrony (mean = 0.94) compared with regional species synchrony (mean = 0.41; Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure.

claim: The regional population CV was positively related to gamma diversity in correlation and regression analyses.
source: Although correlation (Appendix 1—figure 2a) and regression (Figure 4b) analyses showed that the regional population CV was positively related to gamma diversity, this was not supported by the final path analysis model (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The positive relationship between regional population CV and gamma diversity was not supported by the final path analysis model.
source: Although correlation (Appendix 1—figure 2a) and regression (Figure 4b) analyses showed that the regional population CV was positively related to gamma diversity, this was not supported by the final path analysis model (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by path analysis results shown in figure.

claim: The local population CV was positively related to alpha diversity.
source: However, the local population CV was positively and the local species synchrony negatively related to alpha diversity (Figure 3a, Figure 4f and g).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The local species synchrony was negatively related to alpha diversity.
source: However, the local population CV was positively and the local species synchrony negatively related to alpha diversity (Figure 3a, Figure 4f and g).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Local species synchrony increased with the local precipitation CV.
source: Local species synchrony increased with the local precipitation CV but no relations between the regional community CV or its other components and climatic variation were found (Figure 3a, Figure 4h and i).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: No relations between the regional community CV or its other components and climatic variation were found in the all-species analysis.
source: Local species synchrony increased with the local precipitation CV but no relations between the regional community CV or its other components and climatic variation were found (Figure 3a, Figure 4h and i).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: For upscaling pathway I using dominant species, the regional community CV was positively related to local community CV and regional community synchrony with explanatory power reduced to 0.71 from 0.98 for the analysis using all species.
source: For the upscaling pathway I, the regional community CV was positively related to local community CV and regional community synchrony (step B), with the explanatory power reduced to 0.71 from 0.98 for the analysis using all species (comparison of Figure 3b with Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by comparison of path analysis results shown in figures.

claim: For upscaling pathway I using dominant species, the local community CV was positively related to the local population CV and to local species synchrony.
source: The local community CV in turn was positively related to the local population CV and to local species synchrony (step A; Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure.

claim: For upscaling pathway II using dominant species, the regional community CV was positively related to the regional population CV and regional species synchrony with explanatory power reduced to 0.69 from 0.98 for the analysis using all species.
source: For the upscaling pathway II, the regional community CV was positively related to the regional population CV and regional species synchrony (step B), with the explanatory power reduced to 0.69 from 0.98 for the analysis using all species.
evidence: Supported by comparison of path analysis results.

claim: For upscaling pathway II using dominant species, the regional population CV was positively related to the local population CV and regional population synchrony.
source: The regional population CV was positively related to the local population CV and regional population synchrony.
evidence: Supported by path analysis results.

claim: For dominant species, the local population CV was increased by alpha diversity.
source: However, for dominant species, the local population CV was increased by alpha diversity and reduced by larger mean values of precipitation (Figure 3b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: For dominant species, the local population CV was reduced by larger mean values of precipitation.
source: However, for dominant species, the local population CV was increased by alpha diversity and reduced by larger mean values of precipitation (Figure 3b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Both upscaling pathways showed gradually increasing stability from low to high organization levels due to species insurance effects and spatial insurance effects.
source: We investigated ecosystem stability across ecological hierarchies with two alternative upscaling pathways (Wang et al., 2019), and both of them showed gradually increasing stability from low to high organization levels due to species insurance effects and spatial insurance effects of populations and communities, caused by asynchronous dynamics among species and localities (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by path analysis results shown in figure.

claim: The observed patterns are consistent with recent studies carried out at single sites constructing multiple adjacent plots within meta-communities in grassland ecosystems.
source: These patterns are consistent with recent studies carried out at single sites constructing multiple adjacent plots within meta-communities in grassland ecosystems (Hautier et al., 2020; McGranahan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Wilcox et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019)
evidence: Comparison with published literature.

claim: The observed patterns are consistent with recent studies at the regional scale in marine ecosystems.
source: and at the regional scale in marine ecosystems (Lamy et al., 2019; Thorson et al., 2018)
evidence: Comparison with published literature.

claim: The observed patterns are consistent with recent theoretically proposed positive invariability–area relationships.
source: as well as recent theoretically proposed positive invariability–area relationships (Isbell et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with theoretical predictions from published literature.

claim: At large spatial scales, spatial heterogeneity is important in maintaining stability.
source: These results suggest that, at large spatial scales, spatial heterogeneity is important in maintaining stability; losing this heterogeneity (Fahrig et al., 2011; Gámez-Virués et al., 2015) can impair stability.
evidence: Inference from study results with supporting citations.

claim: Losing spatial heterogeneity can impair stability.
source: These results suggest that, at large spatial scales, spatial heterogeneity is important in maintaining stability; losing this heterogeneity (Fahrig et al., 2011; Gámez-Virués et al., 2015) can impair stability.
evidence: Inference from study results with supporting citations.

claim: Species insurance effects (local species asynchrony) were stronger in maintaining stability at the regional scale than the spatial insurance effects of distant populations and communities.
source: We found that species insurance effects (local species asynchrony; Tilman et al., 2014; Yachi and Loreau, 1999) were stronger in maintaining stability at the regional scale than the spatial insurance effects of distant populations and communities despite the large extent and thus expected spatial heterogeneity of our study region.
evidence: Inference from study results with supporting citations.

claim: The finding that species insurance effects were stronger than spatial insurance effects is consistent with a recent investigation in marine plant communities.
source: This result is consistent with a recent investigation in marine plant communities (Lamy et al., 2019) but different from that in fish communities (Thorson et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison with published literature.

claim: The finding that species insurance effects were stronger than spatial insurance effects is different from that in fish communities.
source: This result is consistent with a recent investigation in marine plant communities (Lamy et al., 2019) but different from that in fish communities (Thorson et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison with published literature.

claim: Region-wide synchronous variation in precipitation (mean = 0.86, ranged from 0.62 to 1.00) potentially decreased the spatial heterogeneity and increased the relative importance of the species insurance effect.
source: In our study, the region-wide synchronous variation in precipitation (mean = 0.86, ranged from 0.62 to 1.00) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) potentially decreased the spatial heterogeneity and increased the relative importance of the species insurance effect.
evidence: Inference from observed data shown in figure.

claim: The regulation of spatial insurance effects on the stability of fish communities at regional scale may result from their high mobility.
source: The regulation of spatial insurance effects on the stability of fish communities at regional scale may result from their high mobility.
evidence: Speculative explanation for differences between fish and plant communities.

claim: Fish can move toward their preferred environmental conditions, causing more variable spatial population patterns than those found in plants, potentially strengthening the spatial insurance effects.
source: Fish can move toward their preferred environmental conditions, causing more variable spatial population patterns than those found in plants, potentially strengthening the spatial insurance effects.
evidence: Speculative explanation for differences between fish and plant communities.

claim: The strong species insurance effect suggests that regional community stability to a large part reflects the stability of local communities.
source: In plant communities, the strong species insurance effect suggests that regional community stability to a large part reflects the stability of local communities, which have predominantly been considered in previous studies (Ma et al., 2017; Tilman et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: Inference from study results with supporting citations.

claim: The observed negative species richness–local population stability relationship is in line with theoretical and experimental studies.
source: The observed negative species richness–local population stability relationship is in line with theoretical and experimental studies (Lehman and Tilman, 2000; Tilman, 1999; Tilman et al., 2014, Tilman et al., 2006)
evidence: Comparison with published literature.

claim: Competition between coexisting species for resources in species-rich communities leads to low population stability.
source: proposing that competition between coexisting species for resources in species-rich communities leads to low population stability.
evidence: Theoretical explanation from published literature.

claim: The observed positive species richness–local species asynchrony relationship is expected by theory based on the higher probability of species-rich communities to contain species that are different in responding to environmental fluctuations.
source: The observed positive species richness–local species asynchrony relationship is also expected by theory based on the higher probability of species-rich communities to contain species that are different in responding to environmental fluctuations (Tilman et al., 2014; Yachi and Loreau, 1999).
evidence: Comparison with theoretical predictions from published literature.

claim: Some studies found significant influences of species diversity on stability and asynchrony at scales beyond local.
source: Some studies found significant influences (e.g., Hautier et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2021; Qiao et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: Summary of published literature.

claim: Some studies found no influences of species diversity on stability and asynchrony at scales beyond local.
source: and others found none (e.g., Wilcox et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Summary of published literature.

claim: It has been argued that investigations within a single site or multiple sites with nonstandardized experimental protocols may mask stabilizing effects of species diversity at regional scale.
source: It has been argued (Hautier et al., 2020) that investigations within a single site (Zhang et al., 2019) or multiple sites with nonstandardized experimental protocols (Wilcox et al., 2017) may mask stabilizing effects of species diversity at regional scale.
evidence: Summary of argument from published literature.

claim: This study used a multisite dataset across a large region with a standardized survey protocol but still could not detect significant effects of species diversity at the regional scale.
source: However, even though this study used a multisite dataset across a large region with a standardized survey protocol, it still could not detect significant effects of species diversity at the regional scale (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by study results shown in figure.

claim: The highly uneven distribution of species abundances could in part have been responsible for the lack of diversity effects at regional scale.
source: The highly uneven distribution of species abundances could in part have been responsible for this (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference with supporting citation.

claim: Even when only dominant species were considered, the expected relationship between species diversity and regional asynchrony and stability could not be found.
source: Nevertheless, even when only dominant species were considered, we could still not find the expected relationship between species diversity and regional asynchrony and stability.
evidence: Supported by study results.

claim: In natural grassland ecosystems with high unevenness, species may have co-evolved over time to maintain high stability at a level of species diversity established over a longer time span.
source: It is conceivable that in natural grassland ecosystems, which are often characterized by high unevenness (Dee et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2009; Smith and Knapp, 2003), species have co-evolved over time in such a way as to maintain high stability at a level of species diversity established over a longer time span.
evidence: Speculative explanation with supporting citations.

claim: A history of co-occurrence led to greater community stability in response to a flooding event in a long-term grassland biodiversity experiment.
source: This observation has been made in a long-term grassland biodiversity experiment, where a history of co-occurrence led to greater community stability in response to a flooding event (van Moorsel et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Repeated exposure to drought led to increased species complementarity in response to drought in a long-term grassland biodiversity experiment.
source: and repeated exposure to drought led to increased species complementarity in response to drought (Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The absence of strong species diversity–stability relationship at regional scales in observational studies is not the same as rapid biodiversity loss from an established level typically simulated in experiments.
source: The absence of strong species diversity–stability relationship at regional scales in observational studies is not the same as rapid biodiversity loss from an established level typically simulated in experiments.
evidence: Inference distinguishing observational from experimental contexts.

claim: Regional species loss in the study area due to land-use and climate change in the future may still pose a threat to regional grassland stability.
source: By extension, regional species loss in the study area due to, for example, land-use and climate change in the future may still pose a threat to regional grassland stability.
evidence: Speculative inference about future scenarios.

claim: The strong influence of precipitation on the productivity of different species may have weakened insurance effects of species diversity in this study.
source: The strong influence of precipitation on the productivity of different species (Zhang et al., 2017) may have weakened insurance effects of species diversity in this study.
evidence: Inference with supporting citation.

claim: Strong fluctuations in precipitation in dry grassland may force similar responses among different species, decreasing the dissimilarity and thus compensatory dynamics among species.
source: Strong fluctuations in precipitation in dry grassland may force similar responses among different species, decreasing the dissimilarity and thus compensatory dynamics among species.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed patterns.

claim: The speculation that precipitation fluctuations decrease compensatory dynamics is supported by the low local species asynchrony under high precipitation fluctuation.
source: This speculation is supported by the low local species asynchrony under high precipitation fluctuation (Figure 3a, Figure 4h).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Decreased local population stability under low precipitation means may be due to the decreasing mean-to-standard deviation ratio caused by dominant-species biomass production being more steeply related to precipitation amount than to its standard deviation.

evidence: Description of study methods.
